issues.legal_issue: Prior government sanction is required before taking cognizance of alleged offences against public servants when the charged conduct has a reasonable connection with the discharge of their official duties.
material_facts: The accused were public servants whose official roles included processing, approving, or communicating the proposed transfer of the property.
The prosecution alleged that the officials conspired to transfer the property unlawfully and obtain an undue pecuniary benefit.
The charge-sheet alleged that the offences were committed in the discharge of the officials’ duties.
The trial court took cognizance and issued summons without prior sanction from the Central Government.
issues.conclusion: The required prior sanction had not been obtained, so the cognizance order and criminal proceedings against the appellants were quashed; the appeals were allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure protects qualifying public servants from prosecution for alleged offences committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of official duty. The court must examine the nature of the alleged act and its connection to official functions: there must be a reasonable, not fanciful or pretended, connection, and the act must be directly concerned with the official duty such that it could reasonably be claimed to have been done by virtue of the office. The protection is not limited to proper performance; an act alleged to be dishonest may still be an official act for this purpose. Whether sanction is required depends on the facts and the quality of the act, not merely the offence charged. Sanction must precede cognizance, and the issue may be considered at any stage. The court relied on R.R. Chari v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli v. State of Bombay, Amrik Singh v. State of Pepsu, Hori Ram Singh v. Emperor, H.H.B. Gill v. The King, Matajog Dobey v. H.C. Bhari, Satwant Singh v. State of Punjab, Baijnath Gupta v. State of Madhya Pradesh, B. Saha v. M.S. Kochar, and Prakash Singh Badal v. Union of India. It applied Section 197 CrPC to the allegations of conspiracy under Section 120B IPC and held that sanction from the Central Government was required before cognizance was taken.

rule.if: public_servant_prosecution and official_duty_connection and cognizance_challenged and prior_sanction_absent

predicates.public_servant_prosecution: The accused persons were public servants prosecuted for alleged offences.
predicates.official_duty_connection: The prosecution alleged conduct connected to the accused persons’ official functions, and the alleged acts could reasonably be claimed to have been done in the course of those functions.
predicates.cognizance_challenged: A court took cognizance and issued process against the accused, and that step was challenged.
predicates.prior_sanction_absent: The competent government authority had not given prior approval for the prosecution.
predicates.cognizance_and_proceedings_quashed: The cognizance order and the criminal proceedings are set aside.

issues.definition: When public servants challenge cognizance in a prosecution involving conduct reasonably connected to their official functions, and prior government approval is absent, the cognizance order and proceedings are set aside.
